newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Sharp OK, Howard the real target.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH - Sharp OK, Howard the real target.

text.p: Australian Transport Minister John Sharp, accused of improperly inducing a government board member to quit her job, is quite safe.
The Labor opposition's real target is Prime Minister John Howard's prized reputation for propriety.
If Sharp tried to use a publicly paid job as a lure to move someone from another such job then he has committed an offence.
That would require his departure, but the Labor opposition cannot show it. The evidence is not there, the government's lawyers said on Wednesday.
Labor has tacitly accepted all of that and has notably failed to call for Sharp's resignation.
Instead Labor is trying for a consolation prize -- creating a suspicion that Sharp may have acted improperly.
But even this looks fairly weak.
The best Labor can hope for is that this accusation leaves a nasty odor, which combines with other nasty odors to destroy Howard's reputation for political honesty.
Labor has three obstacles in establishing its case. It has to make people think that:
--Sharp did it.
--It was wrong in principle.
--It was not justified by practical considerations.
There is an implication that the government was trying to use a government job offer to remove Gabi Hollows, a member of the board of the Civil Aviation Safety Authority.

Labor revealed on Wednesday that Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron had written to Hollows expressing an interest in giving her a job in his area, for which she had some qualification. Sharp had no problems with her departure from the aviation board, Herron told Hollows.
Moreover, Sharp himself says that the board needs more aviation expertise and that Hollows has none.
But as noted above, there is no conclusive evidence that that was the government's motive in offering the job.
Even if people were satisfied that that was what the government was up to, not many would be troubled.
There's a hint in there of throwing around public money for political purposes, but from another perspective it just looks like trying to rearrange public staffing.
And this is where the government might even profit from the accusation: Sharp, a former pilot, has a powerful argument that the board needed to be changed.

Asked why he persisted with efforts to get the board to resign, he said in parliament: "Well, I'll tell you why and it is because I am absolutely utterly committed and passionate about improving aviation safety in this country."
He had known all but one of seven people killed a few years ago in an air crash put down to poor safety regulation, he said.
"One of the major contributing causes of that crash was the failure of the safety regulator to properly maintain safe aviation standards in this country."
He had predicted another crash due to lax safety standards and another had indeed happened.

"And who were on the (safety authority's) board? People that the Labor government had appointed. Who was responsible, who was responsible for aviation safety in the country at the time? None other than the Labor government, people sitting here now."
Only one member of the board has any aviation expertise, Sharp says, arguing that this has contributed to the lack of supervision.
It's a strong practical argument. Labor might be smearing Howard's reputation, but it is also drawing attention to a government initiative that many people would praise.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2370
